abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of disability and mortality, with secondary injury mechanisms involving neuronal death and neuroinflammation, for which effective treatments remain limited. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are implicated in post-TBI neuropathology. Cuproptosis, a copper-dependent cell death pathway characterized by mitochondrial oxidative stress, dysfunction, and disrupted dynamics, has recently been implicated in neurological disorders. This study aims to investigate whether NETs exacerbate secondary brain injury by promoting neuronal cuproptosis after TBI and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanism. We observed elevated NET levels in brain tissues from both TBI patients and mice, which correlated with poor prognosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed a significant upregulation of transthyretin (Ttr) in neurons post-TBI. Mechanistically, NETs deliver lactylated S100a9 (S100a9K26la), a glycolysis-dependent lactylated protein, to neurons. S100a9K26la translocates to the nucleus and promotes Ttr transcription. Increased neuronal Ttr protein then competes with ATPase copper transporting β (Atp7b) for binding to copper metabolism MURR1 domain-containing 1 (Commd1) at the W123 residue. This competition disrupts the Commd1-Atp7b interaction, impairing copper efflux and leading to intracellular copper accumulation, mitochondrial oxidative stress, aggregation of DLAT, loss of Fe-S cluster proteins, and ultimately neuronal cuproptosis. Neuron-specific Ttr conditional knockout ameliorated neuronal death, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and neurological deficits in a TBI model. Conversely, inhibition of cuproptosis with the copper chelator tetrathiomolybdate (TTM) yielded similar protective effects. In summary, our findings elucidate a novel pathway wherein NETs, via delivery of S100a9K26la, drive neuronal Ttr overexpression. Ttr disrupts copper homeostasis by interfering with the Commd1-Atp7b axis, ultimately triggering neuronal cuproptosis and exacerbating secondary injury after TBI. This study identifies NETosis and the Ttr/Commd1/Atp7b axis as potential therapeutic targets for mitigating TBI-induced damage.

title: Antiglycation approach in selected autoimmune diseases: Where do we stand?
abstract: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and their receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) have emerged as potential contributors to autoimmune pathology by linking metabolic stress, oxidative injury, and chronic inflammation. This review summarizes current mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence on the role of the AGE-RAGE axis in selected autoimmune diseases, with a focus on systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, psoriasis, and multiple sclerosis. Across these conditions, increased AGE accumulation, enhanced availability of RAGE ligands, and altered soluble RAGE buffering appear to be recurring features associated with disease activity, organ damage, vascular complications, and immune dysregulation. Mechanistically, AGE-RAGE signaling amplifies nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT), and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-dependent pathways, promotes pro-inflammatory immune phenotypes, and may contribute to neoepitope generation and epitope spreading. We also discuss anti-glycation strategies, including carbonyl scavengers, AGE formation inhibitors, redox-modulating agents, crosslink breakers, and RAGE-targeting interventions. Although several compounds show promising anti-inflammatory and antiglycation effects in experimental models, autoimmune-specific translational evidence remains limited, and most studies do not include validated AGE/RAGE biomarkers. Overall, the AGE-RAGE axis represents a plausible therapeutic target in autoimmunity, but establishing its therapeutic potential will require standardized biomarker panels and well-designed clinical trials.

title: Identification of shared and divergent molecular pathways linking ambient air pollutants to mortality and major chronic diseases through proteomic profiling
abstract: Ambient air pollutants have been associated with increased risks of mortality and chronic diseases; however, population-based evidence on their shared versus pollutant- and outcome-specific molecular mechanisms remains unclear. Leveraging proteomics data from 48,645 participants in the UK Biobank, we characterized proteomic signatures related to overall and individual air pollutants, including particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx), and examined their associations with risks of mortality and major chronic diseases. Subsequently, we investigated potential mediating proteins underlying these associations to determine relevant biological mechanisms through functional annotation analyses. Plasma proteins jointly associated with four air pollutants were commonly enriched in immune regulatory pathways, while proteins uniquely associated with PM2.5, PM10, NO2, and NOx were enriched in pollutant-specific pathways of vascular dysfunction, DNA damage, apoptosis signaling, and extracellular matrix remodeling, respectively. Proteomic signatures of air pollutants captured biological processes underlying mortality and major chronic diseases. Mediation analyses and Mendelian randomization identified mediating proteins causally associated with their respective health outcomes, highlighting shared mechanisms of inflammation and immune response as well as outcome-specific pathways such as vascular remodeling for cardiovascular disease, oxidative stress for chronic kidney disease, and cell adhesion for dementia. Specifically, cell-type and tissue enrichment annotation revealed outcome-relevant specificity of advanced glycosylation end product-specific receptor (AGER) for chronic respiratory disease and lung cancer. This study dissects the relationship between ambient air pollutants and adverse health outcomes by revealing both shared and divergent mechanisms and representing potential targets such as AGER for disease prevention and therapeutic intervention.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in OSAHS and associated comorbidities: Mechanism and potential targeted therapeutic strategies
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) is associated with multisystem comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, and neurological, pulmonary, and kidney diseases. Current studies have revealed that the pathophysiology of OSAHS and its associated comorbidities is complex. However, chronic intermittent hypoxia-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are considered to play an important role. In recent years, mechanisms of interaction between mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress have gained attention and have emerged as important potential therapeutic targets. Future delivery systems may improve the tissue or mitochondrial targeting of investigational agents, although their efficacy and safety in OSAHS remain to be established. This review highlights the mutual reinforcement and positive feedback loop between mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, and provides an overview of the current research on associated therapeutic drugs, their novel delivery systems, and development potential. Our review aims to provide new ideas and methods for the treatment of OSAHS-associated comorbidities.

title: Protein S-nitrosylation in the heart: Mechanisms, physiological roles, and pathological remodeling
abstract: Protein S-nitrosylation (SNO), a reversible nitric oxide (NO)-dependent post-translational modification to reactive cysteine residues, finely tunes cardiac excitation–contraction coupling, mitochondrial function, and stress responses. In cardiomyocytes, compartmentalized NO signaling via neuronal (nNOS), endothelial (eNOS), and inducible (iNOS) isoforms regulates SNO of key proteins (e.g., RyR2, LTCC, SERCA2a, mitochondrial Complex I). Under physiological conditions, SNO modulates Ca 2+ handling, myofilament sensitivity, and bioenergetics, while pathological SNO dysregulation, hypo-nitrosylation in heart failure (HF) with reduced ejection fraction or hypernitrosylation in HF with preserved ejection fraction, contributes to contractile dysfunction, arrhythmias, and mitochondrial impairment. Cardioprotective SNO (e.g., during ischemia-reperfusion) acts as a "redox shield", preventing irreversible oxidation of critical cysteines, whereas excessive or mislocalized SNO can be detrimental, this dynamic modification plays an essential role in maintaining cardiac function. However, disruption of NO bioavailability and redox balance during cardiovascular disease alters the cardiac S-nitrosoproteome, contributing to maladaptive signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, contractile impairment, and pathological remodeling. Increasing evidence also highlights the dual nature of SNO exerts either protective or detrimental effects depending on the molecular context, subcellular localization, and disease stage. This review summarizes current knowledge on SNO mechanisms in the heart and discusses its roles in physiological cardiac function and major cardiac pathologies.

title: CLPP loss confers sex-specific protection from renal ischemia reperfusion injury
abstract: Renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is initiated by a burst of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species generated when ischaemia-accumulated succinate is rapidly oxidised upon reperfusion, driving reverse electron transport and triggering lipid peroxidation-dependent tubular cell death. Here, we identify the mitochondrial matrix protease CLPP as an unexpected regulator of renal redox resilience. CLPP deficiency reduced succinate-driven mitochondrial H 2 O 2 production and protected kidneys from functional decline, tubular necrosis, mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, and lipid peroxidation following IRI. Protection was most pronounced in females, in which CLPP loss established a constitutive antioxidant and detoxification programme prior to injury, characterised by increased glutathione and γ-glutamylcysteine abundance, enhanced NADPH-generating pentose phosphate pathway activity, sustained sulfur amino acid metabolism, and elevated capacity for lipid aldehyde detoxification. During reperfusion, these adaptations preserved thiol-redox buffering, limited 4-hydroxynonenal accumulation, and reduced oxidative modification of cysteine residues on proteins involved in complement, coagulation, fibrinolysis, and inflammatory signalling, thereby restricting ferroptotic lipid damage and downstream thrombo-inflammatory amplification. Although reduced reverse electron transport-derived ROS contributed to this phenotype, it was insufficient to account for the sex bias. While CLPP deficiency amplified an endogenous female antioxidant programme, male kidneys, lacking equivalent glutathione-centred preconditioning, showed only marginal benefit. These findings establish mitochondrial proteostasis as a determinant of sex-dependent redox adaptation and identify CLPP as a candidate target for preconditioning against predictable ischaemic insults, including kidney transplantation and cardiac surgery.

title: The ribonuclease ZC3H12A stabilizes BRCA1 mRNA in DNA damage response
abstract: ZC3H12A is an endoribonuclease that destabilizes target transcripts by recognizing stem-loop structures containing a pyrimidine-purine-pyrimidine loop. Here, we identify ZC3H12A as a constitutive stabilizer of BRCA1 mRNA that supports DNA repair capacity. Under basal conditions, depletion of ZC3H12A shortens the half-life of BRCA1 mRNA, reduces its ribosomal loading and lowers BRCA1 protein levels, whereas overexpression has the opposite effect. ZC3H12A binds to the BRCA1 transcript via its PilT N-terminal (PIN) and CCCH-type zinc finger (ZF) domains; enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (eCLIP) narrows the bound sequence to defined intervals that lie outside the canonical stem-loop element through which ZC3H12A recognizes inflammatory transcripts. Moreover, ionizing radiation induces TBK1-dependent phosphorylation of ZC3H12A at Ser386, accompanied by the export of ZC3H12A from the nucleus and its redistribution to cytoplasmic ribosomes. Phosphorylated ZC3H12A occupies a broader region of BRCA1 transcript without promoting its degradation, thereby further prolonging its half-life and increasing its ribosomal loading. As a result, under genotoxic stress, the supply of BRCA1 increases, thereby supporting RAD51 recruitment and homologous recombination repair. These findings identify ZC3H12A as a post-transcriptional regulator of BRCA1 mRNA and show how Ser386 phosphorylation amplifies a protective function that is already present before damage.

title: Proteomic analysis of oxidative modifications in human atherosclerotic plaques and control arteries
abstract: Cardiovascular disease is a major cause of worldwide mortality. A prime underlying cause is atherosclerotic plaque formation at specific arterial locations. Considerable evidence links plaques with chronic inflammation and leukocyte activation, with this potentially resulting in enhanced oxidant-mediated damage to arterial proteins. In this study, human carotid artery plaques and control tissue (superior thyroid artery) were analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for the presence of post-translational modifications (PTMs) generated by redox reactions on proteins. Of 7150 proteins detected across all samples, 2724 carried at least one PTM, with these including mono- and di-oxidation at methionine, tryptophan and histidine, conversion of cysteine to cysteic acid, chlorination and nitration of tyrosine and tryptophan, as well as carbamylation of lysine and N-terminal amines. Higher PTM levels were detected on proteins from plaques compared to control artery tissue, but similar modification types were detected. Elevated concentrations of PTMs were detected in plaques classified as unstable compared to stable, consistent with PTMs being associated with plaque instability. The levels of several PTMs correlate with the concentration of the neutrophil-derived heme protein myeloperoxidase, implicating this enzyme and its oxidants in protein damage, though direct causality has not been established except for chlorination. Large numbers of PTMs were detected on key metabolic proteins including those involved in glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, the pentose phosphate pathway, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Particularly high levels were detected on glycolytic enzymes, including glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) and Complex V subunits consistent with perturbations to cellular metabolism in atherosclerotic plaques.

title: The fruitfly Drosophila melanogaster as an in vivo model of ferroptosis
abstract: Ferroptosis is a non-apoptotic iron-dependent form of cell death involved in cancer, ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation and neurodegeneration. Ferroptosis can be triggered by inhibiting system Xc-, a cystine/glutamate antiporter system, at the plasma membrane (class 1 e.g. erastin) resulting in glutathione depletion or by inhibiting glutathione peroxidase 4 (class 2 e.g. RSL3) resulting in direct lipid peroxidation. In vivo models for ferroptosis are very desirable. We here investigated the effects of erastin and RSL3 on the lifespan, iron metabolism and lipid abundance of the fruitfly Drosophila melanogaster. Both compounds dose-dependently shortened the lifespan of three commonly used fly strains. The reduction in lifespan induced by erastin was rescued by the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1. Erastin had no effect on total glutathione levels but increased the Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio and reduced the amount of ferritin in male but not in female w1118 flies. Also RSL3 only altered the lipid composition of male but not female flies. The fly ortholog of GPX4, Gtpx, has a cysteine instead of a selenocysteine in its otherwise very homologous active center and possesses thioredoxin and not glutathione peroxidase activity. We found that its complete knockout in flies is lethal. Supplying food with ferroptosis inhibitors did not rescue homozygous Gtpx knockout flies suggesting that lethality occurs during early development. Together these results characterize male w1118 flies as a suitable in vivo model for ferroptosis.

title: Corrigendum to “Inorganic nitrate and nitrite ameliorate kidney fibrosis by restoring lipid metabolism via dual regulation of AMP-activated protein kinase and the AKT-PGC1α pathway” [Redox Biol. 51, (2022), 102266]
USP18/DDX5 axis ameliorates mitochondrial morphofunctional damage via OPA1 to inhibit neuronal apoptosis after traumatic brain injury
abstract: BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of mortality and morbidity and a major contributor to loss of working capacity in young adults. Current therapeutic options for TBI remain limited. This study aimed to assess the potential role and therapeutic value of ubiquitin-specific protease 18 (USP18) in TBI. METHODS: and Thy1-Cre mice. A recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 9 carrying Usp18 under control of the hSyn promoter was injected into wild-type mice. Mechanical stretch injury-exposed HT22 cells subjected to a well-established stretch injury model were used to simulate TBI in vitro. The underlying molecular mechanism was explored through bulk-RNA sequencing, immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (MS) analysis, RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing, and RNA immunoprecipitation assays. RESULTS: Multi-omics analysis of mouse brain and RNA-seq profiling of human brain tissues indicated that the expression of the deubiquitinating enzyme USP18 was substantially decreased in hippocampal neurons. Neuron-specific overexpression of Usp18 via recombinant adeno-associated virus 9 (AAV9) led to reduced neuronal apoptosis and improved cognitive performance in mice. The RNA-seq analysis revealed that Usp18 overexpression enhanced the homeostasis of mitochondrial dynamics, ameliorated neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction, and suppressed oxidative stress injury. These results were also confirmed in a well-established mechanical stretch injury model in HT22 cells. Moreover, compared with control mice, neuron-specific Usp18 knockout mice displayed more severe mitochondrial morphological disarray and neuronal damage after TBI. RNA sequencing, MS analysis, RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing, and RNA immunoprecipitation assays mechanistically revealed that USP18 directly interacted with DEAD-box helicase 5 (DDX5) and deubiquitinated and stabilized DDX5 at the K470 residue (via K48-linked ubiquitination) to increase the stability of the Opa1 mRNA, thereby impeding mitochondrial morphofunctional defects. Collectively, the results of this study reveal the protective effect of and molecular mechanism regulating USP18 in TBI pathology and reveal a novel neuron-specific USP18-DDX5-OPA1 axis involved in TBI. CONCLUSIONS: We identified a USP18-promoted mechanism that maintains the homeostasis of mitochondrial dynamics through the DDX5-OPA1 axis in a TBI model; this pathway inhibits neuronal apoptosis and improves cognitive function in mice, suggesting that USP18 activation or AAV9-Usp18 delivery represents a potential therapeutic strategy for TBI.

title: Redox-driven PCK1 sulfenylation: An early warning signal for progression from metabolically healthy obesity to diabetes
abstract: Sustained upregulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis is a major source of hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes, and obesity is the primary driver. However, a substantial subset of obese individuals does not progress to diabetes, a condition termed metabolically healthy obesity, and the underlying mechanism has long remained unclear. ROS act both as physiological signals and as pathological drivers, but no molecular marker characterizes the transition between these two states, making it difficult to time antioxidant intervention against oxidative modification-mediated damage. Here we show that the activity of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a key enzyme of gluconeogenesis, is redox-sensitive. Excess accumulated ROS induce reversible sulfenylation at cysteine 288, near the catalytic center, directly driving gluconeogenesis in the absence of insulin. We therefore propose a dual regulatory model of glucose metabolism signaled by hepatic oxidative load. At low oxidative load, ROS activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) via glutathionylation to promote glycolysis, whereas once the load accumulates, PCK1 is activated via sulfenylation to drive gluconeogenesis, accompanied by a decline in AMPK glutathionylation. Hepatic oxidative load therefore acts as a switch governing the direction of hepatic glucose flux. In diabetic mice, the two modifications show a complementary, stage-dependent distribution paralleling this accumulation, with AMPK glutathionylation predominating in the compensatory stage and PCK1 sulfenylation becoming dominant as the load accumulates further. Their reciprocal dynamic therefore serves as an early warning signal for the transition of ROS from physiological to pathological states. On this basis, we intervened as oxidative load began to accumulate, and found that lowering hepatic ROS prevented the oxidative activation of PCK1, suppressed gluconeogenesis and ameliorated hyperglycemia. These findings reveal that the key gluconeogenic enzyme is directly regulated by redox signals independently of insulin, providing a molecular basis for the heterogeneity of diabetes progression in obesity and for the precise timing of antioxidant intervention.

title: NEURL1-mediated K63-ubiquitination of SLC40A1 drives ferroptosis resistance in pathological scars: Therapeutic targeting via autophagy-activating microneedles
abstract: Ferroptosis resistance contributes to pathological skin scarring, but the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identified a novel selective autophagy pathway NEURL1-SQSTM1/p62-SLC40A1 that controls fibroblast ferroptosis and scar formation. SLC40A1 is upregulated in human scars, conferring ferroptosis resistance by promoting iron efflux. Mechanistically, NEURL1 mediates K63-linked ubiquitination of SLC40A1, enabling its recognition by SQSTM1 for lysosomal degradation. A microneedle system co-delivering curcumin (autophagy activator) and siSLC40A1 effectively activates this axis, induces ferroptosis, and alleviates scarring in vivo. Our findings reveal a new therapeutic target and strategy for pathological scars.

title: PRMT5 promotes ferroptosis in cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury through WDR5/ACSL4 pathway
abstract: The epigenetic mechanisms driving the transition to ferroptosis in acute kidney injury (AKI) remain unclear. In this study, protein methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) and its partner MEP50 were significantly upregulated in the renal tubules of AKI patients and murine models. Genetic silencing of PRMT5 via AAV-shRNA in vivo and siRNA in vitro improved renal function, attenuated mitochondrial damage, and suppressed ferroptotic tubular cell death. Mechanistically, PRMT5 promotes ACSL4 expression in a WDR5-dependent manner, facilitating tubular ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of PRMT5 (GSK591) post-treatment or cloperastine hydrochloride prophylactic administration similarly improved renal function and limited ferroptotic cell death. These findings offer novel insights into the upstream epigenetic regulation of ACSL4-driven ferroptosis and suggest that PRMT5-ACSL4 axis might be a potential therapeutic target for AKI intervention.

title: Disruption of p62 ubiquitination by α-methylene-γ-butyrolactone enhances Keap1 lysosomal degradation for ulcerative colitis therapy
abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an intestinal inflammatory disorder primarily driven by M1 macrophage activation and oxidative stress. p62/Sequestosome-1, a multifunctional autophagy adaptor protein, plays a critical role in regulating autophagy and inflammation. α-Methylene-γ-butyrolactone (αMγB), a conserved structural motif found in anti-inflammatory sesquiterpene lactones from traditional medicinal herbs, was shown to suppress M1 macrophage activation and inflammation. This study aimed to investigate the role of p62 in UC pathogenesis and evaluate the therapeutic potential of αMγB. We found that genetic deletion of p62 aggravated disease severity in both acute pneumonia and UC mouse models. Treatment with αMγB alleviated UC symptoms by reprogramming macrophage polarization, reshaping the mucosal immune microenvironment, and suppressing inflammatory crosstalk between macrophages and epithelial cells. Mechanistically, αMγB covalently modified p62 at C291, preventing its ubiquitination and stabilizing it, which enhanced Keap1 binding and drove its autolysosomal degradation. This process released Nrf2, facilitated its nuclear translocation, and activated the expression of downstream antioxidant and anti-inflammatory genes. Importantly, αMγB established a positive feedback loop between Nrf2 and p62 that sustained p62 upregulation and further promoted Keap1 autolysosomal degradation. These protective effects were abolished in p62 (C291S) mutant mice or upon Nrf2 inhibition. Collectively, our findings demonstrated that αMγB ameliorated UC by specifically targeting p62 at C291, promoting its stabilization, and enhancing Keap1 degradation, thereby modulating macrophage polarization. These findings highlighted the therapeutic potential of αMγB and suggested that augmenting p62 function might represent a promising strategy for UC treatment.

title: Tyrosine nitration: An emerging mechanistic landscape in neurodegeneration and cardiopulmonary disease
abstract: Protein tyrosine nitration is a post-translational modification associated with conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress, driven by the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS). Once considered primarily a footprint of oxidative damage, tyrosine nitration is increasingly recognized as a selective modification that, in specific biological contexts, can alter protein structure, stability, enzymatic activity, and interaction networks. Mechanistically, nitration occurs through peroxynitrite-dependent and heme-peroxidase-dependent pathways and preferentially targets specific tyrosine residues based on local protein structure, solvent accessibility, and microenvironmental chemistry. Accumulating evidence has identified disease-specific nitration signatures across multiple pathological contexts. In neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, nitration of proteins such as tau, α-synuclein, manganese superoxide dismutase, ATP synthase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, heat shock proteins, and cytoskeletal components contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation, metabolic failure, and neuronal loss. Similarly, in cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases, protein tyrosine nitration disrupts vascular and epithelial homeostasis by impairing endothelial signaling, fibrinolysis, lipid metabolism, and barrier integrity through modification of key regulatory proteins. By influencing phosphorylation-dependent signaling, enzymatic function, and protein-protein interactions, tyrosine nitration contributes to the connection between redox imbalance and progressive cellular and tissue dysfunction. This review summarizes current mechanistic insights into site-specific protein tyrosine nitration, highlights the emerging disease-associated nitroproteome, and discusses how advances in analytical and structural approaches are redefining nitration as a functional regulatory modification. Understanding the molecular determinants and consequences of tyrosine nitration may enable the development of targeted diagnostics and therapeutic strategies across diverse human diseases.

title: State-matched redox nanomedicine for cell fate control and multicompartment therapeutic windows
abstract: Tumors persist under sustained redox stress by coupling increased reactive-species production to antioxidant buffering, metabolic plasticity and multicellular support. This creates therapeutic vulnerabilities whose tractability depends on the biological state of the exposed compartment. Here, we frame redox nanomedicine as state-matched manipulation of oxidant flux, antioxidant buffering, oxygen and substrate availability, localization, duration and spatial coverage. We propose that therapeutic outcome emerges from chemistry, exposure and the presence of an executable redox dependency together with the machinery required for adaptation, apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis or cuproptosis. Redox perturbations also propagate through immune, vascular, stromal and metabolic compartments, generating both therapeutic benefits and liabilities. We therefore integrate redox-state dependence, cell-fate assignment, multicompartment effects and translational target engagement into a unified framework. A state-matched development strategy begins with a defined biological dependency, measures local exposure and target engagement, and uses pharmacokinetic, safety and biomarker data to refine product design and patient selection. This framework positions redox nanomedicine as mechanistically testable control of tumor redox states within a defined therapeutic window.

title: Targeting the Ero1α-PDI oxidative protein folding pathway as a broad-spectrum strategy against coronavirus
abstract: The rapid mutation of the SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein promotes immune evasion and challenges current therapeutics. However, its cysteine/disulfide bond pattern is highly conserved across coronaviruses and essential for its structure and function. Here, we demonstrate that the folding and maturation of the S protein is a redox-sensitive process managed by sulfhydryl oxidase Ero1α and protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) in the endoplasmic reticulum. Reducing agents or cysteine mutations inhibit furin-processing of the S protein and its transport to the plasma membrane. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of the Ero1α-PDI pathway impairs S protein oxidative folding, furin cleavage and plasma membrane localization, as well as its fusogenic activity. Using a SARS-CoV-2 reverse genetics model, we confirm that targeting the Ero1α-PDI pathway exhibits potent antiviral effect. Moreover, the Ero1α-PDI pathway is essential for S protein maturation across different β-coronaviruses. Thus, our findings highlight the oxidative protein folding machinery as a promising target for developing broad-spectrum anti-coronavirus therapies.

title: Corrigendum to “VSMC-derived 3HAA activates AhR to drive abdominal aortic aneurysm formation via the p62–Nrf2 axis” [Redox Biol. 95, (2026), 104256]
HDAC1-mediated SUCLA2 lysine β-hydroxybutyrylation modulates myocardial mitochondrial function in sepsis-induced heart dysfunction
abstract: Background Lysine β-hydroxybutyrylation (Kbhb) is associated with energy regulation and mitochondrial function, and its role in sepsis-induced heart dysfunction has not been elucidated. Objectives Reveals the extensive effects of Kbhb in sepsis-induced heart dysfunction and identifies the potential targets. Methods A septic heart dysfunction rat model was induced by lipopolysaccharide intraperitoneal injection. Proteomic and β-hydroxybutyrylomic analyses were conducted to assess alterations in Kbhb between cardiac tissues from the control and lipopolysaccharide rats. Putative regulatory proteins were identified by leveraging a multifaceted hybrid learning framework combined with protein language models. Lysine to arginine (R) mutation was made to mimic decreased Kbhb level. Transcriptomic analysis was further performed to predict the potential downstream mechanism. Results Succinate-CoA Ligase ADP-Forming Subunit Beta (SUCLA2) was selected because of its role in mitochondrial function, and the Kbhb levels of K444 site was significant difference. Decreased Kbhb level at K444 of SUCLA2 was confirmed in septic cardiac tissues and lipopolysaccharide-treated H9c2 cardiomyocytes using specific antibody. SUCLA2 K444R mutant reversed the protective effects of SUCLA2 WT on mitochondrial function in lipopolysaccharide-treated H9c2 cardiomyocytes, accompanied by decreased succinyl-CoA synthetase activity, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, suppressed adenosine triphosphate production, and increased reactive oxygen species accumulation. The aggravating effects of the SUCLA2 K444R mutant on septic heart dysfunction were confirmed in vivo using specific promoter. Mechanistically, histone deacetylase 1 promoted SUCLA2 Kbhb at K444 residue. Conclusions Reduced SUCLA2 Kbhb level at K444 site aggravates myocardial mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to sepsis-induced heart dysfunction. This study reveals a novel function of Kbhb in sepsis-induced heart dysfunction and elucidates the mechanism of SUCLA2 K444 Kbhb.

title: HnRNPK suppresses macrophage-driven inflammation in autoimmune myocarditis by restraining NCF1-dependent oxidized phospholipid signaling and ferroptosis-related changes
abstract: NADPH oxidase-dependent ROS production, oxidized phospholipid (OxPL) signaling, and macrophage ferroptosis are emerging drivers of inflammatory cardiac injury, yet the upstream regulatory mechanisms governing these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K (HnRNPK), a multifunctional RNA-binding protein, as a post-transcriptional regulator of macrophage oxidative stress and ferroptosis-related changes in experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM). HnRNPK was significantly downregulated in EAM cardiac tissues and inflammatory macrophages, whereas AAV-HnRNPK administration attenuated myocardial inflammatory infiltration, fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction and reduced macrophage pro-inflammatory activation. Mechanistically, HnRNPK regulated the balance between NR_104383 and coding Ncf1 transcripts, while NR_104383 knockdown and NCF1 add-back partially reversed its anti-inflammatory effects in BMDMs. NCF1 promoted ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, E06-reactive OxPL signals, mitochondria-associated ER membrane (MAM) remodeling, ER stress, and macrophage ferroptosis-related phenotypes. E06 treatment attenuated NCF1-associated MAM remodeling and partially restored GPX4 expression, whereas oxPAPC increased ER-mitochondria contacts and related molecular changes that were attenuated by E06. Together, these findings establish a functional HnRNPK/NR_104383/NCF1 axis linking alternative transcript regulation to NCF1-dependent redox injury, OxPL-associated MAM remodeling, and ferroptosis-related changes in inflammatory macrophages.

title: Systematic validation of BACH1 antibodies enables the identification of BACH1 localisation as predictor of prognosis in early-stage lung cancer
abstract: The transcription factor BACH1 is a key regulator of cellular stress responses, metabolism, and tumour progression, and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in several diseases, particularly metastatic cancer, inflammatory disease and cardiovascular conditions. As interest in BACH1 biology and its clinical relevance grows, the field would benefit from robust, well-characterised reagents enabling reliable detection of BACH1 across diverse experimental platforms, including analysis of human tissue. Establishing such tools is essential for advancing mechanistic studies and recognising the potential of BACH1 as a prognostic biomarker. We performed the first systematic validation of commercially available antibodies against human BACH1 across multiple experimental platforms, including western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and multiplex immunofluorescence. To ensure robustness, we validated antibodies using complementary approaches, including BACH1-knockout and knockdown cell lines, pharmacological modulators of BACH1 stability and localisation, and multiple extraction conditions. Their performance in immunohistochemistry was further tested using fixed cell pellets from wild-type and BACH1-deficient cells. Validated antibodies were subsequently applied to normal human tissues and lung cancer tissue microarrays to investigate BACH1 expression and subcellular localisation, and quantitative multiplex single-cell immunofluorescence analysis was performed in a cohort of early-stage lung adenocarcinoma patients with clinical follow-up. We demonstrate that subcellular localisation of BACH1 in early-stage lung adenocarcinoma correlates with patient prognosis, underscoring its clinical and translational significance. Our study delivers a rigorously validated toolkit for the BACH1 research community, removes a major barrier to progress in the field, and highlights the potential of BACH1 localisation as a biomarker in early-stage lung adenocarcinoma.

title: A novel hydrogen persulfide donor HPD1 alleviated LPS-induced neuroinflammation by modulating glial polarization through TLR4-MAPK/NF-κB pathway
abstract: The biological role of hydrogen persulfide (H 2 S 2 ) has remained elusive due to the scarcity of controllable donors, despite its importance as a reactive sulfur species whose dyshomeostasis drives neuroinflammation. Herein, we employed HPD1, a novel esterase-responsive H 2 S 2 donor, to investigate its anti-inflammatory effects and underlying mechanisms in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated glial cells. HPD1 exhibited superior cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory efficacy over inorganic sodium disulfide (Na 2 S 2 ) and sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS) in BV2 microglia, consistent with its superior and sustained intracellular H 2 S 2 release efficiency. Functionally, HPD1 dose-dependently attenuated LPS-induced cytotoxicity and shifted microglia and primary astrocytes from pro-inflammatory, neurotoxic states toward anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective phenotypes, as characterized by M1-to-M2 and A1-to-A2 marker profiles, respectively. Mechanistically, HPD1 downregulated toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and attenuated mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activation, as evidenced by reduced extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1 and 2 (ERK1/2), p38, and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) phosphorylation in BV2 microglia. In both BV2 microglia and primary astrocytes, HPD1 markedly suppressed the phosphorylation of both the p65 subunit of nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and inhibitor of κBα (IκBα), prevented the proteasomal degradation of IκBα, and blocked the nuclear translocation of p65. Consequently, HPD1 attenuated the release of neuroinflammatory mediators while promoting the production of neuroprotective factors, thereby protecting neuronal HT22 cells against neurotoxicity induced by conditioned medium from LPS-activated BV2 microglia. In vivo, HPD1 reduced serum proinflammatory cytokine levels in both an acute intrathecal LPS-induced neuroinflammation model and a chronic constriction injury-induced neuropathic pain model. Collectively, our findings identify the TLR4-MAPK/NF-κB axis as a potential molecular pathway through which sustained H 2 S 2 delivery by HPD1 reprograms glial phenotypic polarization and promotes neuroprotection. This study provides mechanistic insights into H 2 S 2 signaling and supports the therapeutic potential of controllable H 2 S 2 supplementation for neuroinflammatory disorders.

title: Androgen receptor-regulated ZNF419 modulates ferroptosis sensitivity via the ZDHHC20–GPX4 pathway in prostate cancer
abstract: Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has recently been recognized as a crucial determinant of therapeutic response in prostate cancer (PCa). However, how androgen receptor (AR) signaling regulates ferroptotic susceptibility remains poorly understood. Here, we identify ZNF419, a previously uncharacterized zinc finger protein, as an AR-regulated factor associated with reduced ferroptosis susceptibility in PCa cells. Transcriptomic profiling and functional validation revealed that ZNF419 expression is markedly elevated in PCa and correlates with poor clinical outcome. Promoter-proximal AR occupancy was detected at predicted ARE-containing regions of the ZNF419 locus and contributed to ZNF419 promoter activation in reporter assays, whereas enzalutamide treatment or AR knockdown reduced ZNF419 expression and increased ferroptosis-associated vulnerability. Mechanistically, ZNF419 promotes ZDHHC20 expression and is associated with activation of a candidate downstream enhancer region. ZDHHC20, a palmitoyltransferase, contributes to GPX4 palmitoylation-associated stabilization and limits ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation of GPX4. Pharmacological interference with palmitoylation attenuates ZNF419-associated GPX4 stabilization, whereas ZDHHC20 restoration partially reverses the increased ferroptosis-associated vulnerability of ZNF419-deficient cells. Collectively, our findings support a previously unrecognized AR-associated ZNF419-ZDHHC20-GPX4 regulatory axis that links AR activity to ferroptosis-associated vulnerability. These findings provide a rationale for further investigating whether modulation of this pathway may influence responses to AR-targeted therapy in advanced PCa.

title: Exosomes derived from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells alleviate otitis media in C57BL/6 mice via the miR-149-3p/NOX2 axis
abstract: Otitis media (OM) is a highly prevalent disease leading to hearing loss in children. Current clinical treatment for OM primarily relies on antibiotics; however, the overuse of antibiotics exacerbates bacterial resistance, posing a global public health challenge. Therefore, novel therapeutic strategies for OM are urgently needed. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (hUCMSCs-Exos) have demonstrated significant therapeutic potential in various diseases, but their efficacy in OM remains unclear. In this study, we induced C57BL/6 mice with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to establish an OM mouse model. OM mice were treated with exosomes derived from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUCMSCs-Exos), through two administration methods, tympanic membrane (TM) and tail vein (TV) injection. Our results showed that hUCMSCs-Exos significantly alleviated OM in mice, as evidenced by improved auditory function, reduced middle ear mucosal thickening, decreased purulent exudation, downregulated expression of inflammatory cytokines, and alleviated oxidative stress. Multi-omics analysis revealed significant alterations in NADPH Oxidase 2 (NOX2) expression and its upstream regulator miR-149-3p within the HIF-1 signaling pathway. qRT-PCR and Western blot confirmed that hUCMSCs-Exos upregulated miR-149-3p and suppressed NOX2 expression, thereby reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and consequently alleviating otitis media inflammation. Furthermore, in vivo gain- and loss-of-function experiments demonstrated that miR-149-3p is a key mediator in hUCMSCs-Exos-regulated NOX2 expression and downstream inflammatory responses. Comparative analysis of administration routes revealed that local TM injection yielded superior therapeutic outcomes compared to systemic TV delivery. In summary, our findings indicate that hUCMSCs-Exos may alleviate LPS-induced OM in mice by delivering miR-149-3p to target and inhibit NOX2 expression and its downstream inflammatory cascade, providing a theoretical basis for hUCMSCs-Exos as a novel non-antibiotic therapeutic strategy for OM.

title: Structural basis for cysteine-linked redox-state plasticity in mammalian methionine sulfoxide reductase A
abstract: Methionine sulfoxide reductase A (MsrA) protects proteins from oxidative damage through cysteine-based redox cycling, but how mammalian MsrA is structurally regulated during oxidation and reductive recycling has remained unclear. We report three crystal structures of mouse MsrA (mMsrA) that capture distinct redox states - reduced (3.0 Å), BME-trapped intermediate-like (BTIL; 1.6 Å), and oxidized (1.9 Å) - and reveal an unrecognized layer of regulation centered on Cys107. The BTIL structure visualizes catalytic Cys72 as a mixed disulfide with β-mercaptoethanol (BME) alongside a sulfenic acid at Cys107, a configuration not previously observed. The oxidized structure resolves the canonical Cys72-Cys218 disulfide together with an unexpected Cys107-Cys227 pairing that locks a C-terminal loop into a cap over the active site. LC-MS/MS mapping, MD simulations, activity assays, and thioredoxin (Trx)-trapping experiments converge on a model in which Cys72 drives catalysis, while Cys107-mediated disulfide rearrangement and Cys227-directed Trx entry gate substrate access and enzymatic regeneration - defining a noncanonical oxidized state that expands the mechanistic repertoire of mammalian MsrA under oxidative stress.

title: Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of thioredoxin promotes myocardial injury, infarction and mitochondrial dysfunction: translocation of cytosolic thioredoxin into mitochondria rescue myocardial dysfunction by restoration of cardiac mitochondrial structure and function
abstract: Cytosolic thioredoxin is a protein disulfide reductase that is involved in several redox-related functions within cells. However, the specific role of Trx in cardiomyocytes or endothelial cells in the normal heart remains unclear. We created a Trx-floxed mouse strain (Trx fl/fl ) to specifically understand whether deletion of Trx in cardiomyocytes or endothelial cell would have specific detrimental myocardial effects. We show that specific deletion of Trx in cardiomyocytes of adult mice ( Trx fl/fl ;αMHC-Cre (Tam ) ) caused severe ischemia and infarction along with heart mitochondrial dysfunction and significant mortality within 3 weeks. In contrast, mice with deletion of Trx in the endothelial cells ( Trx; fl/fl ;VECad-CreER T2(Tam) ) survived with significant decrease in nitric oxide (NO) production due to dysfunction of nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). In rescue experiments, Trx fl/fl ;αMHC-Cre (Tam) or Trx; fl/fl ;VECad-CreER T2(Tam) mice treated with human recombinant thioredoxin (rhTrx) rescued altered mitochondrial structure and function with improved heart function. Further, rhTrx restored the expression of mitochondrial genes and proteins and Ogg1 activity. Taken together, our study demonstrates a critical role of Trx within the cardiac mitochondria and endothelial cells that rescue myocardial dysfunction due to deletion of Trx in cardiomyocytes as well as endothelial cell by rescue of mitochondrial structure, function, and improving eNOS function within the heart.

title: Benzene exposure in relation to the development of glycemic dysregulation and type 2 diabetes mediated by oxidative stress and aggravated by inflammation in a repeated-measure prospective cohort study of Chinese adults
abstract: Aims Whether and how benzene (a ubiquitous environmental pollutant posing substantial public health concerns) exposure contributes to glycemic dyshomeostasis and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) remain unclear. Methods Among 3422 Chinese adults from the Wuhan-Zhuhai cohort, urinary N-Acetyl-S-(phenyl)-L-cysteine (PMA; dependable benzene exposure biomarker) was repeatedly measured at baseline and 3-year follow-up to investigate its associations with glycemic homeostasis markers (fasting plasma glucose [FPG] and insulin [FPI], homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance [HOMA-IR], insulin resistance [IR], and impaired fasting glucose [IFG]) and T2DM appropriately by performing general linear, logistic, and Poisson regression models. Oxidative stress (exhaled carbon monoxide [eCO]; urinary 8-hydroxy-2’-deoxyguanosine and 8-iso-prostaglandin-F2α; plasma protein carbonyl) and inflammation (plasma C-reactive protein [CRP]; mean platelet volume [MPV]; neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR]) biomarkers were detected to explore their roles by performing mediation and interaction analyses. Results Cross-sectionally, positive PMA-FPG (β=0.014, 95% confidence interval: 0.005∼0.024), PMA-FPI (0.076, 0.049∼0.104), PMA-HOMA-IR (0.090, 0.059∼0.122), PMA-IR (odds ratio=1.516, 1.192∼1.929), PMA-IFG (1.653, 1.164∼2.343), and PMA-T2DM (1.445, 1.019∼2.045) associations were discovered. Longitudinally, positive PMA-FPG (β=0.059, 0.016∼0.101) and PMA-HOMA-IR (quartile 4 vs. 1: 0.054, 0.002∼0.106; P trend =0.041) associations were uncovered, and participants with consistently high PMA level had higher risks of incident IR (risk ratio=2.513, 1.638∼3.857) and T2DM (2.834, 1.042∼7.708). PMA-CRP and PMA-MPV interactions on FPG, PMA-CRP interaction on IFG, and PMA-NLR interaction on T2DM were detected. 8-hydroxy-2’-deoxyguanosine and eCO mediated 4.74% and 5.97% of the PMA-FPI and PMA-T2DM associations, respectively. Conclusions Benzene exposure of general adults was linked to the development of glycemic dyshomeostasis and T2DM possibly through mediation by oxidative stress and interaction with inflammation.

title: LncRNA CCDC152 coordinates a tumor-associated selenoprotein P cycle that sustains selenium-dependent redox homeostasis in glioblastoma
abstract: Selenium is essential for the synthesis of redox-active selenoproteins, including glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a central suppressor of ferroptosis. However, how malignant cells coordinate selenium acquisition and reutilization to maintain redox homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a tumor-associated selenoprotein P (SELENOP) cycle in glioblastoma (GBM) that is coordinated by the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) CCDC152. Highly proliferative GBM cells secrete SELENOP, recapture it through LRP8, and reutilize selenium to maintain intracellular selenoprotein abundance and cell proliferation. Disruption of SELENOP or LRP8 suppressed GBM cell proliferation, while LRP8 depletion reduced GPX1 and GPX4 abundance and its intracellular domain was required for growth-promoting activity. Unexpectedly, although CCDC152 suppresses SELENOP translation in hepatocyte-derived cells, it positively regulated SELENOP production, LRP8 expression, and intracellular GPX1 and GPX4 abundance in GBM cells. CCDC152 depletion also increased ferroptosis susceptibility. Clinical analyses further showed that elevated expression of SELENOP and CCDC152 was associated with poor prognosis in astrocytoma, IDH-mutant. Together, these findings identify the CCDC152- SELENOP-LRP8 axis as a tumor-adapted selenium utilization system that couples extracellular selenium transport to intracellular redox homeostasis, revealing selenium utilization as a redox vulnerability that may be exploited by ferroptosis-inducing therapies.

title: Glial-specific mitochondrial failure and redox imbalance contribute to regional vulnerability in Friedreich's ataxia
abstract: Abstract Friedreich’s ataxia (FA) is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by reduced expression of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein important for iron–sulfur cluster assembly and mitochondrial homeostasis. Although FA has traditionally been attributed to neuronal dysfunction, increasing evidence suggests that glial cells play a critical role in disease progression, although their contribution remains poorly defined. Using the FXN I151F mouse model, we investigated cell-type–specific metabolic and redox alterations in neurons and glial populations from the cerebrum, cerebellum, and dorsal root ganglia (DRG). Neuronal and glial-enriched fractions were isolated by immunomagnetic separation and analyzed for mitochondrial function, iron metabolism and reactive oxygen species (ROS). The analyses identified the DRG as the most severely affected region, exhibiting early and pronounced mitochondrial respiratory deficits, increased ROS, mitochondrial iron accumulation, lipid peroxidation, and reduced levels of glutathione peroxidase 4 and nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells. These results highlight the vulnerability of sensory neurons and their supporting satellite glial cells. In contrast, in the cerebrum and cerebellum, astrocytes displayed earlier and more severe alterations than neurons, including impaired respiratory chain efficiency, disrupted complex I-III supercomplex interaction, elevated ROS, and hallmarks of ferroptosis. Neuronal abnormalities emerged later, suggesting that glial dysfunction precedes -or drives- neuronal pathology within the central nervous system. Overall, these findings reveal pronounced region and cell-type-specific vulnerabilities in FA and support the importance of targeting glial mechanisms—particularly iron dysregulation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis— as targets for potential therapeutic strategies.

title: Stress-induced vtRNA1-1 modulates redox homeostasis and ferroptosis susceptibility in hepatocellular carcinoma cells
abstract: Ferroptosis is a unique form of regulated cell death characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. Although the molecular details of ferroptosis regulation have been widely explored, the contributions of short non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) to ferroptosis regulation, other than miRNAs, remain poorly understood. Here, we identified vault RNA1-1 (vtRNA1-1) as a previously unrecognized short ncRNA regulator of ferroptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells. vtRNA1-1 expression was upregulated by ferroptosis inducers and exhibited strong negative correlation with ferroptosis sensitivity, thus protecting cells from ferroptosis. vtRNA1-1 levels were elevated in selected ferroptosis-resistant cells, while its depletion reversed the phenotype thus resensitizing these cells to ferroptosis. These findings suggested a contribution of vtRNA1-1 to both intrinsic and acquired ferroptosis resistance. Mechanistically, we uncovered that increased oxidative stress, which potentiates lipid peroxidation, specifically induced expression of the vtRNA1-1 paralog in an NF-κB dependent manner. Elevated vtRNA1-1 levels suppressed NF-κB-mediated pro-oxidant gene expression, thereby limiting reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and alleviating oxidative stress. Taken together, oxidative stress-inducible vtRNA1-1 governs redox balance by forming a reciprocal regulatory loop with NF-κB and this loop determines ferroptosis susceptibility by adjusting basal ROS levels. Our findings provide unprecedented insights into the regulation of redox homeostasis in HCC cells mediated by a short ncRNA and uncovered vtRNA1-1 as a potential therapeutic target for overcoming ferroptosis resistance in liver cancer.

title: CO-mediated restoration of mitochondrial redox homeostasis contributes to alleviating multiple programmed cell deaths in hepatic I/R injury
abstract: Hepatic ischemia–reperfusion injury (HIRI) remains a life-threatening complication in liver surgery and transplantation with no clinically approved therapy. Here we develop a hyaluronic acid-modified, ROS-responsive nanoformulation (CPs@HA) that enables controllable delivery of carbon monoxide (CO) specifically to injured liver tissue. We show that mitochondrial dysfunction is closely associated with three distinct cell death pathways (ferroptosis, cuproptosis, and disulfidptosis) that occur in parallel during HIRI. CPs@HA restores mitochondrial homeostasis through activating the AMPK–SIRT1–PGC-1α axis and restoring Ca 2+ balance, accompanied by suppressed mtROS burst, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), maintained cristae ultrastructure, and restored respiratory complex (I & IV) and PDHC activities. This dual restoration of ATP energy supply and NADPH reducing capacity, together with the direct inhibitory effect of CO on oxidative stress and inflammation, is associated with the attenuation of ferroptosis, cuproptosis, and disulfidptosis, consistent with transcriptomics and functional assays in both hepatic tissues and cellular models. Consequently, CPs@HA effectively attenuates liver injury. By interrupting the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, metabolic collapse, and cell death with mitochondrial repair as a key component, this work suggests a potentially unified therapeutic strategy against HIRI and indicates that targeting mitochondrial homeostasis may help mitigate multiple cell death programs in parallel.

title: Phasic metabolic remodeling coordinates cardiac myofibroblast differentiation and function
abstract: ABSTRACT Fibroblast differentiation into matrix-producing, contractile myofibroblasts is accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, but whether these changes precede differentiation or arise from the activated phenotype remains unclear. We integrated time-resolved extracellular flux analysis, transcriptomics, stable isotope-resolved metabolomics, and metabolic interventions to define the relationship between metabolism and myofibroblast differentiation in adult mouse cardiac fibroblasts stimulated with transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ). TGFβ increased glycolysis within 1.5 h, before broad transcriptional remodeling and induction of periostin and α-smooth muscle actin. Mitochondrial respiration initially declined but increased at 48 h as the phenotype emerged, accompanied by smaller, less elongated mitochondria and greater respiratory capacity. [U- 13 C 6 ]-glucose tracing revealed progressive incorporation of glucose-derived carbon into glycolytic intermediates, nucleotide sugars, and glycerol 3-phosphate, followed later by increased labeling of tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates. TGFβ-treated fibroblasts also demonstrated enhanced insulin-stimulated glycolysis. Replacing glucose with galactose attenuated collagen and periostin induction, whereas glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase inhibition prevented induction of collagen, periostin, and α-smooth muscle actin. Conversely, glucose transporter 1 or mutant PFK2 (Glyco Hi ) overexpression increased glycolysis without inducing myofibroblast markers. Together, these loss- and gain-of-function studies indicate that glycolytic activity is required for complete differentiation but is not sufficient to initiate the phenotype. Inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I or ATP synthase preferentially reduced collagen abundance, while glycolytic and Complex I inhibition diminished TGFβ-induced collagen gel contraction. These findings define a phasic metabolic program in which early glycolytic activation precedes transcriptional and phenotypic remodeling, whereas mitochondrial respiratory capacity increases later and distinct metabolic nodes selectively regulate collagen abundance and contractile behavior.

title: Corrigendum to “Phase IB trial of high dose ascorbic acid + nab-paclitaxel + cisplatin + gemcitabine in patients with untreated metastatic pancreatic cancer” [Redox Biol. 88 (2025) 103895]
abstract: Upon review of their data, the authors identified the issues listed below and self-reported them to the journal.The matter was investigated by Elsevier's Research Integrity & Publishing Ethics team (RI&PE) in accordance with COPE guidelines.Having reviewed the authors' explanation and data, the Editor was satisfied that the corrected analysis resolved the issues.These errors do not impact the original interpretation of the data.The authors would like to apologize for any inconvenience caused.The corrections to these errors are as follows:

title: Endothelial nitric oxide signaling in cellular and systemic metabolism
abstract: Endothelial cell-derived nitric oxide (NO) is best known for its role in the regulation of vascular tone. However, growing evidence shows that endothelial NO acts as a flux- and compartment-dependent redox regulator of cellular and systemic metabolism. NO directly modulates metabolic networks through reversible or irreversible chemical modification of iron centers, reactive cysteine and tyrosine residues as well as fatty acids. Mechanisms of NO-mediated regulation of cellular metabolism include the S-nitrosation of enzymes involved in glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and nucleotide biosynthesis as well as the control of iron and heme availability. NO-derived nitrating species additionally generate electrophilic nitro-fatty acids, which act on metabolic and redox transcriptional programs through reversible cysteine adduction. Moreover, specialized endothelial cells contribute to metabolic regulation across organs, for example lipid trafficking in adipose tissue, iron homeostasis in the liver and erythropoiesis in the bone marrow. Finally, tissue/organ-specific endothelial dysfunction may disrupt organ and systemic metabolic control through multiple mechanisms, raising new questions and therapeutic opportunities. Understanding how cell- and enzymatic source-specific NO signaling defines endothelial heterogeneity and function may provide a mechanistic framework to address organ-specific endothelial dysfunction in cardiometabolic disease.

title: Ellagic acid mitigates follicular atresia in laying chickens via GPX4 upregulation to block ferroptosis and p53 suppression to attenuate DNA damage
abstract: Follicular atresia is a critical factor limiting the reproductive lifespan of laying chickens, a process primarily driven by the progressive death of granulosa cells. This study investigates the precise redox mechanisms underlying chicken follicular atresia and evaluates the cytoprotective efficacy of Ellagic Acid (EA). In vivo and in vitro analyses revealed that this atretic process is executed by a lethal synergy between lipid peroxidation-driven ferroptosis (characterized by mitochondrial collapse and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) depletion) and DNA damage response-triggered apoptosis (characterized by the activation of the p53 signaling axis). EA intervention successfully mitigated this structural and cellular degeneration. Mechanistically, molecular dynamics simulations and cellular thermal shift assays provided compelling biophysical evidence that EA physically binds and structurally stabilizes the active pockets of both GPX4 and p53. The indispensability of this dual-targeting paradigm was validated through siRNA-mediated gene silencing: GPX4 knockdown abrogated EA's ability to restore intracellular glutathione and suppress ferroptosis, while p53 knockdown blunted its anti-apoptotic rescue effects. A double knockdown neutralized EA's protective pleiotropy. In conclusion, chicken follicular atresia is structurally governed by a GPX4/p53-mediated interplay between ferroptosis and apoptosis. EA functions beyond a generic antioxidant as a specific, dual-target pharmacological agent, highlighting targeted redox interventions as a highly viable strategy for preserving the ovarian reserve in laying chickens.

title: Itaconate protects the blood-brain barrier by preserving microvascular bioenergetics after traumatic brain injury
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability, yet effective pharmacological therapies remain unavailable. Early blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption accelerates neuroinflammation and secondary brain injury. It has been well recognized that brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs) depend on mitochondrial oxidative metabolism to maintain BBB integrity. Here, we investigated the role of the mitochondria-derived immunometabolite itaconate in regulating cerebrovascular bioenergetics and BBB integrity after TBI. Using a controlled cortical impact model, we found that TBI induced early Irg1 upregulation but paradoxically reduced fatty acid-derived itaconate levels in brain microvessels (MVs). TBI also created a hypoxic microenvironment that disrupted the Irg1/itaconate axis in BMECs. Genetic Irg1 deficiency exacerbated microvascular metabolic dysfunction, particularly deficits in fatty acid oxidation (FAO), and BBB breakdown, whereas treatment with 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI) restored mitochondrial metabolism/bioenergetics in brain MVs within 12 h after injury and preserved BBB integrity. Mechanistically, TBI and hypoxia suppressed carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1a), whereas 4-OI restored CPT1a expression, enhanced FAO, and activated Nrf2 signaling, thereby preserving tight junction proteins and VE-cadherin in hypoxia-exposed human BMECs. Together, these findings identify itaconate as a critical regulator of endothelial mitochondrial metabolism and BBB integrity following TBI and support therapeutic targeting of the Irg1/itaconate pathway to prevent secondary neurovascular injury.

title: eNOS uncoupling drives oxidative stress and arrhythmogenic vulnerability in experimental hypothyroidism
abstract: Aims Cardiac arrhythmias are a major cause of morbidity and sudden cardiac death worldwide, and hypothyroidism has emerged as an important risk factor. Among the mechanisms involved in cardiac electrical stability, nitric oxide (NO) signaling, particularly via endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), plays a critical role in cardiac excitation–contraction coupling. Here, we investigated whether hypothyroidism increases susceptibility to stress-induced arrhythmias through eNOS uncoupling and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Methods and Results Hypothyroidism was induced in Swiss mice by methimazole administration in the drinking water for 21 days. In vivo electrocardiographic recordings revealed a marked increase in stress-induced arrhythmias following dobutamine/caffeine challenge. At the cellular level, left ventricular cardiomyocytes from hypothyroid mice exhibited elevated ROS production, electrical instability, enhanced Na + and Ca 2+ currents and reduced repolarizing K + currents, resulting in action potential prolongation. Oxidative stress was associated with redox-dependent CaMKII activation, contributing to intracellular Ca 2+ instability and triggered activity. Mechanistically, hypothyroidism promoted eNOS uncoupling in cardiomyocytes, evidenced by a reduced eNOS dimer/monomer ratio, leading to increased ROS generation and impaired nitric oxide production. Pharmacological restoration of eNOS coupling with tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) normalized ROS and nitric oxide at cellular level, attenuated redox-dependent CaMKII activation and significantly reduced arrhythmia incidence in vivo . Conclusion Together, these findings demonstrate that eNOS uncoupling is a key driver of oxidative stress and arrhythmogenic vulnerability in experimental hypothyroidism, suggesting that restoration of eNOS coupling may represent a potential therapeutic strategy to reduce arrhythmogenic risk in hypothyroidism.

title: O-GlcNAc transferase promotes TGF-β-induced extracellular H2O2 production through a p38-p47phox-NOX2 axis
abstract: ABSTRACT Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive interstitial lung disease characterized by aberrant transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling leading to excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. Reactive oxygen species (ROS), produced downstream of TGF-β signaling, propagate tissue damage and fibrogenesis. Metabolic reprogramming of lung fibroblasts is essential for fibrogenesis, yet the mechanisms linking nutrient/stress sensing to ROS production remain poorly understood. The O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) is a nutrient/stress-sensitive enzyme that adds O-GlcNAc moieties to substrates. We previously demonstrated that loss of OGT reverses bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice. In this study, we hypothesized that OGT modulation would broadly affect intracellular signaling in lung fibroblasts. Using unbiased kinomics and molecular profiling, we demonstrated that pharmacologic inhibition of OGT suppressed TGF-β-induced phosphorylation of p38, but not ERK or JNK. We identified p38 as a novel O-GlcNAc substrate and found that OGT inhibition blunted its TGF-β-induced phosphorylation, which was associated with less downstream activation of p47 phox . The OGT-p38-p47 phox axis was upregulated in a non-resolving mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis, and OGT blockade reduced TGF-β-induced extracellular H 2 O 2 production in lung fibroblasts via a p47 phox -NOX2-dependent mechanism. These findings establish OGT as a metabolic regulator of non-canonical TGF-β signaling and NOX2-dependent ROS production in lung fibroblasts providing a novel mechanistic link between nutrient/stress-sensing and redox signaling in lung fibrosis.

title: Isoenzyme-specific determination of glutathione peroxidase activity in cell lysates and GPX1/GPX4-HiBiT cellular target engagement
abstract: Glutathione peroxidases (GPX) are primarily selenoproteins that maintain cellular redox balance. GPX1, GPX2 and GPX4 are associated with cancer progression and treatment resistance, but the lack of isoenzyme-specific cellular assays has limited evaluation of GPX-targeting compounds. As GPX1 and GPX2 share high sequence homology, as well as substrate and inhibitor profiles, their individual activities are difficult to distinguish. Here, we present a glutathione reductase (GR)-coupled assay using auranofin to quantify combined GPX1/GPX2 activity and total GPX activity in crude cell lysates. The method was validated using multiple cell lines, with or without selenium supplementation, spiked human recombinant enzymes, and knockdown cells. Combined GPX1/GPX2 activity correlated with GPX1 protein levels and accounted for the majority of GPX activity in selenium-supplemented cells. GPX4's low catalytic turnover limits the feasibility of measuring its activity in cell lysates, so we established a high-throughput cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) using HiBiT-tagging of GPX1 and GPX4 in HT1080 cells to quantify isoenzyme-specific target engagement. Using this new complementary assay platform, we found that ferroptosis inducers RSL3, PACMA-31 and ML-162 destabilized GPX4 in cells, RSL3 and ML-162 destabilized cellular GPX1, but none of these compounds had a strong effect on either total GPX, or GPX1/GPX2 activities in lysates. Additional reported GPX1/GPX2 or GPX4 inhibitors showed minimal GPX4 target engagement, whereas GPX1 was readily targeted in cells. The FDA-approved drugs, ceftibuten and omapatrilat, inhibited GPX1/GPX2 activity more potently than auranofin in cell lysates, suggesting that GPX1/GPX2 suppression may contribute to their cellular effects. Together, these complementary GPX assays presented here provide practical tools for evaluations of specific GPX isoenzyme cellular activities and development of selective GPX-targeted therapies.

title: Modulating the synovial ROS–NO–RNS network attenuates fibroblast-like synoviocyte pyroptosis and osteoarthritis progression
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is characterized by persistent synovial inflammation and disturbed redox homeostasis, yet most redox-directed interventions predominantly target reactive oxygen species (ROS) and provide limited control over the interconnected ROS–nitric oxide (NO)–reactive nitrogen species (RNS) network. Here, we developed Mn@GaMOF, a gallium-based metal–organic framework bearing highly dispersed mixed-valence Mn sites, to coordinately regulate the synovial nitro-oxidative microenvironment. Post-synthetic Mn incorporation markedly enhanced the superoxide dismutase (SOD)- and catalase (CAT)-like activities and peroxynitrite (ONOO − )-scavenging capacity of GaMOF, whereas the GaMOF framework suppressed inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression and excessive NO production. This complementary regulation reduced ROS, NO, and RNS accumulation and attenuated nitro-oxidative stress in inflammatory macrophages and fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLSs). In macrophages, Mn@GaMOF suppressed inflammatory cytokine production and reduced M1-associated inflammatory features while enhancing selected M2-associated markers. In primary FLSs, Mn@GaMOF attenuated nitro-oxidative stress, inflammatory and catabolic activation, wound-closure responses, and NLRP3/caspase-1/GSDMD-associated pyroptosis. Consistently, conditioned medium derived from Mn@GaMOF-treated FLSs under pyroptotic stimulation preserved chondrocyte matrix homeostasis and proliferation while reducing catabolic activation and cellular senescence. In a destabilization of the medial meniscus mouse model, intra-articular Mn@GaMOF alleviated pain-related behaviors and gait abnormalities and mitigated synovitis, cartilage degeneration, osteophyte formation, and subchondral bone sclerosis, accompanied by reduced synovial 3-nitrotyrosine accumulation and NLRP3 expression. Collectively, these findings identify coordinated regulation of the synovial ROS–NO–RNS network as a redox-directed strategy associated with suppression of FLS pyroptosis and pathological synovium–cartilage crosstalk, highlighting this interconnected redox network as a therapeutically relevant axis in OA.

title: KLHL20 protects against aldosterone-induced cardiomyocyte cuproptosis by promoting ubiquitination-mediated MR degradation
abstract: Excessive secretion of mineralocorticoid aldosterone (ALD) and overactivation of mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) are considered major drivers of cardiac remodeling and heart failure in patients with primary aldosteronism. Cuproptosis is a copper-dependent form of regulated cell death that has been implicated in pathological cardiac remodeling. However, its mechanism in ALD/MR-induced cardiac remodeling remains unclear. In this study, it is found that ALD-induced cardiac remodeling is accompanied by copper overload and cuproptosis-associated mitochondrial proteotoxic stress. Kelch like family member 20 (KLHL20) functions as a substrate adaptor of the Cullin3 (CUL3) ubiquitin ligase complex. Its expression is significantly decreased in ALD-stimulated myocardium. Cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of KLHL20 aggravates ALD-induced cuproptosis, myocardial hypertrophy, and interstitial fibrosis. Concurrent treatment with the copper chelator tetrathiomolybdate (TTM) attenuates these aggravated pathological changes. Mechanistically, KLHL20 promotes polyubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of MR, thereby limiting MR protein accumulation and nuclear localization. Consequently, MR-dependent transcription of the copper transporter Solute carrier family 31 member 1 (SLC31A1) is suppressed. As a result, cardiomyocyte copper overload and mitochondrial proteotoxic stress are alleviated. However, sustained ALD stimulation downregulates KLHL20 expression, thereby weakening KLHL20-mediated control of MR protein stability. Cardiomyocyte-specific overexpression of KLHL20 significantly attenuates cardiac remodeling. These findings indicate that KLHL20 is a clinically viable therapeutic target for combating cardiac remodeling.

title: Targeting ERO1α triggers tumor immunosurveillance in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a highly aggressive malignancy with limited responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Here, we identify endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductase 1 alpha (ERO1α; ERO1A), a key regulator of oxidative protein folding, as a determinant of tumor immunogenicity and immunotherapy response in TNBC. Unbiased proteomic profiling demonstrated that ERO1α deficiency remodels the TNBC glycoproteome, leading to enrichment of pathways associated with immune signaling. Although ERO1α loss did not affect tumor cell growth, it reshaped the immune tumor microenvironment, enhancing antigen presentation, altering myeloid-cell composition, and modulating PD-1/PD-L1-associated signaling. Functionally, ERO1α deficiency sensitized otherwise refractory TNBC tumors to PD-1 blockade, resulting in durable tumor regression in immunocompetent hosts. In contrast, ERO1α deletion in bone marrow-derived immune cells had minimal effects on tumor growth or therapeutic response, supporting an ERO1α tumor-intrinsic mechanism. Pharmacologic inhibition of ERO1α with the novel small-molecule inhibitor I29 phenocopied ERO1α genetic deletion and enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy. Together, these findings identify ERO1α-dependent glycoproteome remodeling as a regulator of antitumor immunity and a therapeutically actionable mechanism of immune checkpoint responsiveness in TNBC.

title: Intestinal xdh overexpression promotes organismal aging with early redox dysregulation
abstract: Oxidative stress accompanies aging, but whether a defined endogenous oxidant source can initiate tissue-to-organism aging remains unclear. We investigated xanthine oxidase (XO), an enzyme coupling purine catabolism to superoxide and hydrogen peroxide generation, using a human cross-sectional cohort and Drosophila genetic models. Among 442 adults, higher serum XO activity was independently associated with shorter relative leukocyte telomere length. Ubiquitous overexpression of xdh, the Drosophila xanthine oxidoreductase gene, shortened lifespan, accelerated locomotor decline, disrupted metabolic homeostasis, reduced antioxidant enzyme activities, and remodeled redox-, immune-, and metabolism-related transcriptional programs. Intestine-specific xdh overexpression was sufficient to reproduce organismal lifespan shortening and functional decline in both sexes. Intestinal xdh elevation increased intestinal DCF fluorescence and reduced total superoxide dismutase activity before detectable barrier leakage or expansion of culturable intestinal bacteria. These early redox abnormalities were followed by progressive barrier failure, increased bacterial burden, and reduced survival during hydrogen peroxide challenge. Intestinal transcriptomics further revealed early and persistent enrichment of oxidoreductase, glutathione, immune, and lipid-metabolic programs, with shared functional signatures across intestinal xdh overexpression, systemic xdh overexpression, and chronological aging. Collectively, these findings identify intestinal XO as a defined metabolic source of redox disruption capable of producing effects beyond the gut. They support a model in which sustained intestinal oxidative stress precedes and amplifies the loss of gut homeostasis, linking local redox disturbance to organismal aging phenotypes.

title: Glial lipid reprogramming in brain aging: Lipid identity, organelle stress, and redox vulnerability
abstract: Brain aging is accompanied by progressive glial dysfunction, impaired metabolic adaptation, oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to neurodegenerative disease. Although many studies of lipid metabolism in aging and neurodegeneration emphasize lipid abundance, lipid amount alone cannot explain why glia become redox-vulnerable. This review advances a chemistry-resolved integrative framework in which glial lipid reprogramming is understood through aging- and disease-associated changes in lipid identity, composition, oxidation state, storage form, subcellular localization, and lipid-mediated signaling. We discuss evidence from aged brain tissue, human neurodegenerative disease, iPSC-derived glial systems, and mouse models showing that altered lipid handling in microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells reshapes phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, myelin processing, astrocytic metabolic support, and neuronal injury. We emphasize that acyl-chain saturation, head-group structure, oxidized lipid species, neutral lipid storage, plasmalogen-dependent redox buffering, peroxisomal lipid metabolism, and compartmental distribution determine how lipids regulate receptor engagement, lipid-droplet dynamics, lysosomal stress, mitochondrial function, ferroptotic susceptibility, and inflammatory redox signaling.
