Importantly, glial lipid reprogramming is further shaped by extracellular vesicle-mediated neuron-glia communication, regional lipid heterogeneity, and sex-dependent modifiers of glial metabolism. Oxidative stress therefore reflects the convergence of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-enriched membranes, oxidized phospholipids, oxysterols, ceramide accumulation, plasmalogen loss, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, lysosomal iron release, peroxisomal dysfunction, and declining glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), GTP cyclohydrolase 1-tetrahydrobiopterin (GCH1-BH4), and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-dependent protective systems. Finally, we discuss lipid-centered therapeutic opportunities targeting cholesterol efflux, apolipoprotein E (APOE) lipidation, lipid-droplet metabolism, sphingolipid pathways, lipid peroxide defense, plasmalogen support, extracellular vesicle biology, and lipid-based delivery systems. By shifting the focus from lipid accumulation to lipid identity, compartmental handling, and biological context, this review synthesizes glial lipid reprogramming as an integrative framework linking brain aging to redox-sensitive neurodegeneration.

title: Inhibiting MD2 activates AMPK-dependent PPARγ/NOX4 signaling to attenuate mitochondrial oxidative stress and relieve pulmonary hypertension
abstract: AIMS: Pulmonary hypertension (PH), a severe vascular disorder, is closely associated with chronic inflammatory states and oxidative stress. Myeloid differentiation protein 2 (MD2), a key co-receptor of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), is well established in mediating various inflammation-driven pathologies. However, its role in pulmonary hypertension and its potential involvement in oxidative stress regulation remain unclear. METHODS AND RESULTS: MD2 expression was upregulated in both PH patients and murine PH models. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of MD2 improved hemodynamic parameters, attenuated pulmonary vascular remodeling, and reduced right ventricular hypertrophy. MD2 inhibition significantly reduced mitochondrial oxidative stress in vivo and in vitro. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that suppression of the membrane protein MD2 activated intracellular AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling, leading to enhanced peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) activity. PPARγ, in turn, suppressed nuclear transcription of NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), resulting in a marked reduction in mitochondrial oxidative stress. CONCLUSION: This study indicates that MD2 may act as an upstream regulator of mitochondrial oxidative stress in PH. Inhibition of MD2 attenuates pulmonary hypertension through activation of the AMPK/PPARγ axis, which suppresses NOX4 mediated mitochondrial oxidative stress. Targeting MD2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for PH.

title: Protein disulfide Isomerase-A1 as a novel organizer of Endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane contacts via reticulon 4
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–plasma membrane (PM) contact sites (ER–PMc) are nanodomains essential for ER functions such as Ca 2+ signaling, lipid metabolism, cell signaling and ER stress responses. However, how ER-PMc dynamics relate to protein folding-related ER oxidoreductases is unclear. We hypothesized that ER-PMc are signaling hubs regulated by ER redox chaperones from the Protein Disulfide Isomerase (PDI) family such as PDIA1. We show that PDIA1 co-localizes with ER–PMc and co-immunoprecipitates with the scaffold protein extended synaptotagmin-3 (E-Syt3). E-Syt3 overexpression increases levels of the ER-shaping protein Reticulon-4 (RTN4), which promotes tubular ER formation, and switches RTN4B1 to B2 isoform. These effects occur in parallel with the increased number of ER-PMc, while PDIA1 secretion is mildly impaired, rather than increased. Importantly, PDIA1 silencing increases number and decreases size of ER-PMc, while affecting ER morphology and tubulation and down-regulating RTN4-B expression. Conversely, RTN4 silencing impairs PDIA1 association with ER-PMc. This indicates that PDIA1 sustains RTN4-B-driven ER tubulation and ER-PMc stability, while RTN4 supports PDIA1 targeting to ER-PMc. Functionally, PDIA1 silencing markedly reduces cytosolic calcium influx, and IP3 receptor activation. Together, our findings position PDIA1 as an integral component and new functional organizer of ER–PMc sites. We propose a model in which ER proteostasis, via PDIA1, converges with ER morpho-structure, via RTN4, to integrate redox and Ca 2+ signaling at ER–PM interfaces.

title: Exosomal miR-146a-3p from BEAS-2B cells alleviates NETs-Aggravated asthma by targeting HIF-1α to inhibit ferroptosis
abstract: The molecular mechanism by which hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) regulates asthma pathogenesis through modulation of neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation remains poorly defined. Given that NETs act as core drivers of allergic asthma pathology by amplifying airway inflammation and inducing airway epithelial ferroptosis, this study aimed to elucidate the regulatory axis involving airway epithelial cell-derived exosomal miR-146a-3p. We proposed that exosomal miR-146a-3p directly targets HIF-1α to suppress the transcriptional activity of its downstream target gene ELANE, thereby blocking NETs formation and ultimately alleviating asthmatic airway inflammation. Using public transcriptomic data from asthma patients, we identified miR-146a-3p as significantly downregulated in asthmatic tissues. BEAS-2B cell-derived exosomes were isolated via differential centrifugation. Employing a PMA-induced neutrophil inflammation model and an HDM/NETs-challenged asthmatic mouse model, we systematically demonstrated that BEAS-2B cell-derived exosomes function as efficient delivery vehicles for miR-146a-3p, transporting it into neutrophils. By targeting and inhibiting HIF-1α nucleocytoplasmic translocation and its transcriptional activation capacity, exosomal miR-146a-3p significantly downregulated the expression of NE-key mediator of NET formation-thereby blocking aberrant NETs release. Moreover, we confirmed that NETs reduction modulates the cGAS-STING signaling pathway, reverses the aberrant expression patterns of the ferroptosis regulatory proteins GPX4, SLC7A11, and ACSL4, maintains cellular iron homeostasis, and subsequently alleviates airway epithelial ferroptosis, ultimately ameliorating asthmatic airway inflammation. Collectively, this study reveals a novel mechanism by which excessive NET accumulation exacerbates asthma pathology through cGAS-STING-mediated airway epithelial ferroptosis. Furthermore, it identifies BEAS-2B cell-derived exosomal miR-146a-3p as a key regulatory molecule and potential therapeutic target, offering a new theoretical framework and intervention strategy for understanding and treating allergic asthma.

title: Corrigendum to “Macrophage AMPK activated by oxidative stress drives profibrotic crosstalk with tubular cells to accelerate renal fibrosis after ischemic and reperfusion injury” [REDOX Biol. 90, (2026), 104002]
p22phox-dependent redox pathways contribute to placental oxidative injury and adverse embryonic outcomes following transient gestational hypoxia–reoxygenation
abstract: Placental development occurs in a physiologically low-oxygen environment, but disturbances in oxygen availability may disrupt placental function. Hypoxia followed by restoration of oxygen availability can promote oxidative injury and cellular stress responses; however, the contribution of p22phox-dependent NADPH oxidases to these processes during early placentation remains unclear. We thus investigated placental and embryonic responses to transient gestational hypoxia followed by return to normoxia (TGH) using wild-type mice and mice with global deletion of Cyba , encoding the NADPH oxidase subunit p22phox. In wild-type placentae, TGH increased oxidative DNA damage and lipid peroxidation and was associated with inflammatory signaling, DNA damage response (DDR), unfolded protein response/integrated stress response (UPR/ISR), and apoptosis-associated changes. TGH also altered trophoblast-associated phenotypes and was accompanied by increased embryonic lethality and impaired growth. These stress-associated placental responses were broadly attenuated in p22phox-deficient placentae, alongside improved embryonic outcomes. Furthermore, TGH increased HIF-1α and HIF-2α protein abundance and Vegf mRNA expression in wild-type placentae, whereas these responses were attenuated in p22phox-deficient placentae. Human preeclamptic placentae exhibited partially overlapping molecular signatures, including altered redox status, increases in NADPH oxidase component abundance, oxidative damage, and DDR-, UPR/ISR-, and apoptosis-associated markers. Raman spectroscopy revealed protein- and lipid-associated biochemical differences. Exploratory single-cell transcriptomic reanalysis identified cell type-specific expression of redox- and stress-associated genes and transcriptional differences involving DNA repair, metabolism, and cell-cycle pathways in extravillous trophoblasts. Together, these findings implicate p22phox-dependent redox pathways in placental oxidative injury and cellular stress responses following TGH and identify overlapping redox- and stress-associated signatures in human preeclamptic placentae.

title: NRF2 in hypertrophic scarring: A stage-dependent redox hub poised between resolution and persistence
abstract: Hypertrophic scarring (HTS) is a fibroproliferative outcome of deep dermal injury, reflecting failed scar resolution rather than collagen excess alone. Sustained oxidative and inflammatory signaling is a prominent feature of HTS. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) amplify TGF-β/Smad and NF-κB-linked signaling, reinforce matrix stiffening, and sustain activated fibroblasts within a mechanically loaded niche. However, how NRF2 activity changes across scar maturation-and whether it remains protective, represents a compensatory response, or supports fibroblast persistence-remains unresolved. The KEAP1-NRF2 pathway is a major redox-regulatory node, coordinating antioxidant, detoxification, metabolic, proteostatic, and anti-ferroptotic programs. We propose a testable, stage- and compartment-dependent model rather than a fixed early-to-late switch. Early injury may preferentially engage the redox-sensitive Neh2-KEAP1 arm, whereas growth-factor and mechanical signaling in established scars may increasingly influence NRF2 through the KEAP1-independent Neh6-GSK-3β/β-TrCP arm. Autophagy-linked phospho-p62 (SQSTM1) may provide a separate noncanonical but KEAP1-dependent route to NRF2 stabilization. We synthesize TGF-β/Smad-NOX4 signaling, NF-κB inflammation, p62 feedback, iron-lipid redox and ferroptosis, and mechanoredox coupling-and apply a non-ordinal engagement-to-phenotype (E2P) framework considering disease proximity, NRF2 engagement, causal dependence, scar-relevant phenotype, and replication/methodological quality. Because stage- and cell-resolved nuclear NRF2 data in human HTS are lacking, and disease-proximal evidence for persistence-permissive activity remains limited despite a recent independent gain-/loss-of-function study in human HTS fibroblasts, NRF2 is best viewed as a conditional redox hub rather than a uniformly antifibrotic switch. This framework identifies experiments needed to resolve NRF2 directionality and determine whether stage- and compartment-aware local modulation is therapeutically justified.

title: Loss of T cell-intrinsic Keap1 alleviates colitis by suppressing Th17 differentiation and enhancing regulatory T cell functions
abstract: ABSTRACT Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a form of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by chronic inflammation in the colon. In this study, we elucidate the roles of antioxidation proteins Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) in modulating CD4 + T cell differentiation and intestinal inflammation in UC. Using mice with T cell-specific deletion of Keap1 or Nrf2, we demonstrate that T cell-intrinsic Nrf2 levels influence T helper (Th) cell differentiation, intestinal inflammation and colitis disease outcome. Loss of Keap1 in T cells suppressed proinflammatory Th1 and Th17 subset differentiation, while promoting induced regulatory T-cell (iTreg) generation in an Nrf2-dependent manner, thereby alleviating intestinal inflammation and protecting against colitis. Mechanistic analyses revealed that Keap1 deletion was associated with metabolic reprogramming in iTregs, characterized by increased glutamine utilization and enhanced mitochondrial respiration, suggesting that these metabolic changes may contribute to enhanced iTreg generation. Further, analyses of UC patient tissues and omics datasets revealed increased Nrf2 gene expression and enrichment of Nrf2-associated transcriptional signatures in colonic Tregs, correlating with Foxp3 expression. In summary, our findings identify Keap1-Nrf2 axis as an important regulator of iTreg generation and function, suggesting that targeting this pathway may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for IBD.

title: IL-27 promotes systolic overload-induced cardiac oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, and heart failure development
abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND Interleukin-27 (IL-27) is a heterodimeric cytokine that serves as a bifunctional rheostat rather than an inherently pro- or anti-inflammatory signaling protein. However, the specific role of IL-27 in regulating systolic overload-induced cardiac inflammation and heart failure (HF) pathogenesis remains unknown. METHODS We investigated the effects of genetic IL-27 receptor deficiency (IL-27Rα knockout), pharmacological IL-27 blockade, and recombinant IL-27 administration on transverse aortic constriction (TAC)-induced HF in mice. RESULTS Cardiac IL-27 expression was significantly elevated in both murine and human HF tissues. The global genetic ablation of the IL-27 receptor (IL-27Rα) significantly suppressed TAC-induced cardiac inflammation, fibrosis, hypertrophy, HF progression, and mortality. Corroborating these protective effects, transcriptomic analysis (RNA-seq) revealed that IL-27Rα deficiency drastically suppressed pathways driving immune responses and antigen presentation, alongside the significant downregulation of networks governing systemic inflammation, pathogen infection, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Furthermore, pharmacological neutralization of IL-27 effectively attenuated TAC-induced left ventricular dysfunction, chamber dilation, myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, and leukocyte infiltration. Conversely, the administration of recombinant mouse IL-27 exacerbated the TAC-induced cardiac accumulation of multiple immune cell subsets, resulting in worsened cardiac fibrosis, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and overall HF progression. CONCLUSIONS Our findings demonstrate that IL-27 acts as a critical pathogenic driver of cardiac inflammation and HF development by modulating both cardiac immune cells (predominantly T cells) and non-immune cells, highlighting the IL-27 signaling axis as a promising therapeutic target.

title: Spatiotemporal mapping of free radicals in cells: The scientific legacy of Ronald P. Mason
abstract: Overview of a scientific legacyRonald P. Mason devoted his scientific career to a fundamental and challenging scientific quest: the identification and characterization of highly reactive, short-lived free radicals and the study of their actions in biological systems, both in vitro and in vivo.Over more than four decades at the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS), Mason and his collaborators advanced electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, spin trapping, isotopic labeling, mass spectrometry, immuno-spin trapping, and in vivo radical detection.Their work encompassed xenobiotic metabolism, anticancer drugs, environmental toxicants, oxygen-and nitrogen-centered radicals, transition-metal chemistry, lipid peroxidation, protein-centered radicals, redox signaling, inflammation, oxidative tissue injury, and the spatiotemporal mapping of free-radical reactions in cells and tissues.A defining principle of Mason's research was the rigorous identification and structural characterization of reactive intermediates, rather than the mere inference of "oxidative stress" based on nonspecific measurements.His early studies identified radical intermediates generated during the metabolism of nitroheterocyclic compounds, quinone anticancer drugs, carbon tetrachloride, acetaminophen, alcohol, and other xenobiotics.Subsequent investigations clarified fundamental aspects of Fenton chemistry and established mechanisms by which NADPH oxidases and nitric oxide synthases generate radicals in vivo.His studies of hemoproteins further demonstrated that proteinderived radicals could be detected and characterized unambiguously through EPR spectroscopy, spin trapping, and mass spectrometry.These foundational studies culminated in the development of immuno-spin trapping, an innovative method that enabled DMPOtrapped protein and DNA radical adducts to be detected immunologically and localized within cells and tissues.This novel assay greatly expanded the utility and accessibility of DMPO spin trapping while adding spatiotemporal resolution to the study of free-radical processes in cells.Subsequent work extended these approaches to mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and disease-associated mechanisms of oxidative injury, including the development of novel imaging methods based on immuno-spin trapping.Collectively, Mason's research transformed free radicals from inferred contributors to biological injury into chemically identifiable, mechanistically traceable, and spatially detectable intermediates.Mason's scientific legacy is especially relevant as redox biology moves beyond the generalized and often vague concept of "reactive oxygen species" toward the identification of structurally defined oxidants, molecular targets, and signaling pathways.The analytical rigor he championed will continue to guide emerging areas of biomedical research, including cellular reprogramming and regenerative medicine.

title: Lack of NRF2 expression alters the dynamics of stress granules promoting the aggregation of ALS disease-associated proteins
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron death. Although ALS pathogenesis is multifactorial, increasing evidence highlights a close interplay between dysfunction of RNA metabolism and redox imbalance in disease progression. Redox perturbation converges with RNA dysregulation at the level of the dynamics of stress granules, transient ribonucleoprotein assemblies implicated in protein aggregation, in ALS. The redox-sensitive transcription factor NRF2 ( Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 ) plays a pivotal role in cellular homeostasis, yet its function and regulation remain poorly defined in ALS. In this study, we explore how NRF2 modulates stress granule dynamics under oxidative and non-oxidative stress conditions. Using live-cell imaging, we reveal that NRF2 deficiency enhances the formation of stress granules in response to oxidative and non-oxidative stressors, facilitates their persistence, and promotes increased stress granule recruitment of ALS-linked proteins such as TDP-43 and FUS. Likewise, we uncover a protective role of pharmacological NRF2 activation in limiting exacerbated stress granule responses in iPSC-derived motor neurons from C9orf72 -ALS patients and show how NRF2 activation can impact TDP-43 aggregation and loss of function in SH-SY5Y cells. Together, these findings position NRF2 as a crucial integrator of redox signalling and RNA metabolism in ALS pathogenesis. Targeting NRF2 may offer novel therapeutic avenues to counteract the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, dysfunctional stress granule dynamics, and protein aggregation in motor neuron disease.

title: Neutrophils, NETs, and efferocytosis in aging: A resolution-failure axis driving inflammaging
abstract: Population aging is a defining demographic trend of the 21st century and is accompanied by a rising prevalence of chronic diseases, functional decline, and multimorbidity that impose substantial health and socioeconomic burdens worldwide. This demographic shift is characterized by a fundamental paradox in the immune system: immunosenescence, marked by declining immune function, and inflammaging, a state of chronic low-grade inflammation. While neutrophils are essential for antimicrobial defense and immune surveillance, their broader role in maintaining tissue homeostasis during aging is increasingly recognized. Here, we examine emerging evidence that age-related alterations in neutrophil fate and functional programming, including apoptosis, NETosis, and senescence-associated states, influence macrophage behavior and contribute to persistent inflammation. Recent studies further suggest that interactions between apoptotic neutrophils and macrophages are not merely mechanisms of cellular clearance but active processes that promote macrophage metabolic and functional reprogramming toward inflammatory resolution. We discuss how aging may perturb this neutrophil-macrophage axis through altered neutrophil programming, defective efferocytosis, and impaired resolution responses, while highlighting key unresolved questions regarding senescent neutrophil biology, neutrophil-specific efferocytic signaling, and macrophage metabolic reprogramming in aging tissues. These emerging insights also identify the neutrophil-macrophage resolution axis as a potential therapeutic target for restoring tissue homeostasis and promoting healthy aging.

title: Selenoprotein P and type 2 diabetes risk in a large cohort of older German adults
abstract: Background A previous meta-analysis reported an increased type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk at high blood selenium levels but included few prospective cohorts. Here, we assessed the long-term associations of serum SELENOP concentrations and incident T2D in a large cohort. Methods Serum SELENOP concentrations were measured at baseline and 5-year follow-up in 6,529 participants aged 50-74 years in the German ESTHER study. Multivariable Cox models were performed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for incident T2D across quintiles (Q) of SELENOP concentrations. Results During a median follow-up of 11.5 years (interquartile range, 7.1–16.7 years), 1,235 participants developed T2D. No statistically significant association between time-dependently modelled SELENOP and T2D risk was observed (HR [95%CI] for Q5 vs. Q1, 1.08 [0.89-1.30]). SELENOP concentrations decreased on average by 0.90 mg/L from baseline to 5-year follow-up. For those 80% of the population, for whom SELENOP decreased by less than 1.83 mg/L, a statistically significant 22% lower T2D risk was observed compared to those 20% with a larger SELENOP decrease (HR [95%CI]: 0.78 [0.62-0.98]). Results were consistent across subgroups defined by sex, age, BMI, smoking status, physical activity level, prediabetes, oxidative stress, inflammatory status, and vitamin D status. Conclusions This large prospective cohort study found no increased long-term risk of T2D among older adults residing in Germany with time-dependently modelled SELENOP concentrations. However, although a decrease in SELENOP with ageing is normal, the 20% of the population with the greatest decline in serum SELENOP concentrations showed an increased T2D risk.

title: HIF-3α beyond the dominant-negative paradigm: Isoform diversity, species divergence, and redox-driven diseases
abstract: : Hypoxia-inducible factor 3 alpha (HIF-3α) has long been considered a minor, inhibitory branch of the HIF pathway. However, accumulating evidence suggests that HIF-3α is a context-dependent regulator with transcriptional activator and dominant-negative functions. The human HIF3A locus undergoes extensive alternative splicing, yielding at least eight to ten protein isoforms. In contrast, the mouse Hif3a gene produces only three major variants. This creates substantial species divergence in isoform architecture and expression. Full-length human isoforms, such as HIF-3α1, HIF-3α2, and HIF-3α9, are bona fide transcription factors that regulate both canonical and non-canonical hypoxic targets, including EPO, LC3C, REDD1, SQRDL, and IGFBP-1. In contrast, truncated variants, such as HIF-3α4, antagonize HIF-1/2-dependent angiogenic and metabolic programs in a tissue-specific manner. Mouse models demonstrate that canonical HIF-3α integrates developmental and redox cues in the lungs, heart, and metabolism. Furthermore, human HIF3A methylation and isoform-specific expression have been linked to obesity, liver dysfunction, diabetes, chronic lung disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer. Full-length isoforms often promote tumor growth and metastasis (e.g., in colorectal and pancreatic cancers), whereas truncated isoforms constrain angiogenesis or stabilize oncogenic HIF-2α in certain contexts. In this review, we integrate these findings into an isoform-resolved, cross-species framework that distinguishes experimentally validated HIF-3α functions from indirect associations and proposed redox mechanisms. We propose that HIF-3α acts less as a single hypoxia transcription factor and more as an isoform-specific rheostat that shapes acute, chronic, and redox-stressed states. Finally, we outline the need for long-read transcriptomics, isoform-specific assays, evidence-stratified disease models, and targeted modulation of individual HIF-3α variants to translate this complexity into therapeutic strategies for redox-driven human diseases.

title: Encoding metabolic stress into tumor evolution through ECM–integrin-dependent transcriptional plasticity
abstract: Tumor evolution is driven not only by genetic alterations but also by the capacity of cancer cells to adapt to dynamic microenvironmental stresses. Emerging evidence indicates that metabolic constraints can remodel the extracellular matrix (ECM), extending stress adaptation beyond cell-intrinsic programs. Importantly, stress-induced changes in ECM composition, organization and mechanics may persist beyond the initiating stimulus and influence subsequent cell–matrix signaling. We refer to this proposed persistence of stress-associated extracellular changes as“ECM encoding”, a form of physicochemical information storage that is mechanistically distinct from genetic memory or cell-intrinsic epigenetic stabilization. Here, we critically review the ECM–integrin axis as a signaling interface linking metabolic stress, redox adaptation and transcriptional plasticity. Metabolic pressures, including hypoxia, nutrient limitation and isolation stress, reshape ECM composition, mechanics and ligand availability, thereby reprogramming integrin signaling. Through focal adhesions, cytoskeletal tension and nuclear mechanotransduction, integrin-dependent signals can influence chromatin accessibility and converge with stress-responsive networks involving YAP/TAZ, ATF4, HIF, NRF2, STAT3 and NF-κB. In parallel, matrix-dependent regulation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production and NRF2-mediated antioxidant responses may provide mechanisms linking extracellular cues to redox adaptation. These interconnected processes can promote phenotypic plasticity associated with stemness, dormancy, metastasis, immune evasion and therapeutic resistance, although their relative contributions vary across tumor types and experimental contexts. Finally, we evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting the ECM–integrin–redox network while considering signaling redundancy, previous clinical setbacks and the need for biomarker-guided patient selection.

title: Protein adduction by multiple aldehydes contributes to α-synuclein aggregation and dopaminergic neuron loss in rat models of Parkinson's disease
abstract: Dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the substantia nigra causes the motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease (PD). The mechanisms underlying this neurodegeneration remain unclear. Aldehydes exhibit high reactivity that can covalently modify functional proteins and cause cell damage. This study aimed to characterize protein adduction by endogenous aldehydes and investigate its role in dopaminergic neuron loss in PD. Forty free aldehydes were identified in rat models of PD induced by 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) and rotenone using chemical isotope labeling coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry. Twenty-two aldehydes were found in the rat brain for the first time. In addition to lipid peroxidation, amine oxidation was the major source of aldehydes. Levels of 27 aldehyde-protein adducts in the substantia nigra and striatum were increased by 1- to 5-fold at 4–6 h after 6-OHDA injection. Consistently, most of these protein adducts were significantly increased in the rotenone model. Application of the trapping reagent phenelzine and the aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 activator Alda-1 reduced protein adduction by aldehydes and attenuated neuron loss induced by 6-OHDA injection. Twelve aldehydes covalently modified α-synuclein in 6-OHDA-treated rats, with the lysine residue in the GLSK peptide identified as the primary binding target. Aldehydes caused peptide crosslinking and aggregation of α-synuclein. Additive effects of covalent modification by aldehydes contributed to neuron death. Collectively, protein adduction by multiple aldehydes contributes to α-synuclein aggregation and dopaminergic neuron loss in rat models of PD. Multiple biogenic aldehydes, especially those from abnormal oxidation of amines, represent a novel class of toxic molecules that play a pathogenic role in PD.

title: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase prevents bleomycin-induced lung injury and fibrosis by degrading oxidized phospholipids
abstract: The pathogenesis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a life-threatening disease, has not been fully elucidated. Conditions such as senescence, infection, allergy, or exposure to chemical or radiation agents can compromise the alveolar epithelial barrier, potentially leading to dysregulated tissue repair and subsequent fibrogenesis. We have previously demonstrated that acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH), a eukaryotic lipase, prevents induction of inflammasome activation by degrading oxidized phospholipids (oxPLs). In the present study, using a bleomycin (BLM)-induced murine model of lung injury and fibrosis, we found that AOAH played a protective role by reducing pulmonary oxPL abundance and suppressing NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activation. Providing oxPL-neutralizing antibody E06 or exogenous AOAH significantly attenuated BLM-induced inflammasome activation, inflammation, and fibrosis. These findings suggest that oxPL-induced NLRP3 inflammasome activation is a critical driver of BLM-induced lung injury, and that AOAH limits lung pathology by degrading oxPLs. Increasing pulmonary AOAH abundance represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of IPF.

title: Multi-organ proteomics identifies oxidative stress pathways underlying genetic and pharmacological SGLT2 suppression
abstract: BackgroundSodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors provide clinical benefits beyond glycaemic control, although the underlying systemic mechanisms remain incompletely understood.MethodsWe performed proteomic profiling across eight metabolically relevant tissues and plasma in high-fat diet-fed mice with either genetic deletion (SGLT2−/−) or pharmacological inhibition (dapagliflozin) of SGLT2. Differentially expressed proteins were analysed using Gene Ontology, KEGG pathway enrichment, and integrative clustering. Cross-species validation was performed using plasma and skeletal muscle proteomic datasets from patients with type 2 diabetes treated with dapagliflozin.ResultsBoth genetic and pharmacological SGLT2 inhibition induced widespread tissue-specific proteomic remodelling, particularly in liver, adrenal glands, and adipose tissue. Enrichment analyses consistently identified oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and metabolic pathways as dominant processes. Shared protein signatures across conditions were strongly linked to reactive oxygen species regulation, mitochondrial respiration, and glutathione metabolism. Tissue-specific analyses revealed divergent responses, including increased oxidative pathways in liver and adrenal tissue, but reduced oxidative signalling in adipose tissue and heart. Cross-species analyses confirmed conservation of oxidative stress and mitochondrial pathways in human plasma and skeletal muscle following SGLT2 inhibition.ConclusionsSGLT2 inhibition induces coordinated multi-organ proteomic remodelling characterised by conserved oxidative stress and mitochondrial signatures, supporting a systemic mechanism underlying the pleiotropic benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors.

title: Cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation promotes oxidative stress and neurotoxicity through Trx1 mRNA sequestration and translational suppression
abstract: Transactive response (TAR) DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a multifunctional DNA/RNA binding protein. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation is a pathological hallmark of diverse neurodegenerative diseases collectively termed TDP-43 proteinopathy. Oxidative stress is closely associated with TDP-43 aggregation and neurotoxicity in TDP-43 proteinopathy, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain elusive. To delineate molecular basis of TDP-43 proteinopathy, we conducted deep quantitative proteomic profiling using Neuro-2a (N2a) neuronal cell model of TDP-43 proteinopathy overexpressing human wild-type TDP-43 (N2a-hTDP-43). We identified thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) as a central node linking mitochondrial dysfunction and redox dysregulation to TDP-43 proteinopathy. Consistent with this, TDP-43 overexpression markedly reduced Trx1 protein levels. Moreover, inhibiting Trx1 exacerbates, whereas overexpressing Trx1 alleviates, cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation and neurotoxicity in N2a-hTDP-43 cells. Furthermore, overexpressing Trx1 alleviates TDP-43-associated pathologies in mouse primary neurons. Notably, we identified that cytoplasmic TDP-43 proteins sequester Trx1 mRNAs into insoluble inclusions, leading to its translational suppression. We also demonstrated that suppression of Trx1 is a core mechanism eliciting oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in TDP-43 proteinopathy. Importantly, in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (MN) harboring the pathogenic TDP-43 M337V mutation (TDP-43M337V iPSC-MNs), Trx1 expression is downregulated, concomitant with increased oxidative stress, compared to the isogenic TDP-43WT iPSC-MN control. Furthermore, inducing Trx1 expression markedly reduces oxidative stress and cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation in TDP-43M337V iPSC-MNs, suggesting conserved neuroprotective role of Trx1 in TDP-43 proteinopathy in human. Collectively, we identified Trx1 as a pivotal regulator of TDP-43 proteinopathy, highlighting therapeutic potential of Trx1 for TDP-43 proteinopathies.

title: Air Pollution Leaves a Redox-Proteomic Imprint: From Shared Inflammation to Disease-Specific Vulnerability

title: RUNX1-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy regulates hepatocyte ferroptosis by promoting SLC25A28 degradation
abstract: Lambda-cyhalothrin (LCT), a commonly used pyrethroid insecticide, has been increasingly considered as a possible risk factor for liver injury. Ferroptosis, a form of regulated cell death resulting from the accumulation of iron and lipid peroxidation, is identified by mitochondrial dysfunction, but its mechanisms underlying LCT-induced liver damage remain poorly defined. Runt-related transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) isa transcription factor involved in diverse developmental and stress-responsive processes, yet its role and regulation in xenobiotic-induced liver injury remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether RUNX1-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy links mitochondrial iron homeostasis to ferroptosis-associated liver injury following LCT exposure. We showed that LCT exposure induced structural and functional liver injury accompanied by ferroptosis, impaired autophagic flux, and defective BNIP3-mediated mitophagy. Mechanistically, LCT suppressed RUNX1 expression, resulting in decreased BNIP3 transcription and consequently compromising mitophagic clearance of the mitochondrial iron importer SLC25A28. The resulting iron accumulation, glutathione imbalance and lipid peroxidation could contribute to ferroptosis and accelerate hepatocellular senescence. Of note, RUNX1 or BNIP3 overexpression efficiently restored mitophagy and promoted SLC25A28 turnover, thereby suppressing ferroptosis and cellular senescence. However, these benefits were abolished by BNIP3 knockdown or SLC25A28 overexpression. The results further identified SLC25A28 as an important downstream mediator of BNIP3-mediated mitophagy. Together, these findings identify that RUNX1 represents an important regulatory factor involved in LCT-induced liver injury by regulating BNIP3-dependent mitophagy and facilitating SLC25A28 turnover, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis and attenuating hepatocellular senescence. Our study uncovers that modulation of the hepatic RUNX1-BNIP3-SLC25A28 axis may represent a potential strategy for mitigating LCT-induced liver injury.
